item.title: What to Know About Lula’s Election Victory in Brazil, and What Comes Next
item.description:
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil won re-election on Sunday, according to official preliminary results, punctuating a string of conservative wins across Latin America. His right-wing opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to accept the outcome.

Mr. Lula became the first presidential candidate since 1989 to win after finishing second in the opening round. In just three weeks, he added more than 10 million votes, gaining ground across the country.

Mr. Lula received 51.8 percent of the vote, compared with 48.2 percent for Mr. Bolsonaro, with nearly all ballots counted. Mr. Bolsonaro called for the election to be annulled after a judge extended voting hours by two hours, a change that both campaigns had requested.

Here’s what to know:

Mr. Lula accomplished what no candidate had done since Brazil restored direct presidential elections in 1989: He won after finishing second in the opening round this month. In each of the nine preceding elections, the first-round leader won the presidency, either outright or in a runoff.

Mr. Lula tried and failed to overcome such a deficit in 1989. After finishing second to Fernando Collor de Mello, he rallied support from defeated rivals and surged in the polls. He ultimately lost in the runoff, 53 percent to 47 percent.

His victory on Sunday added another reversal to an extraordinary political career. Mr. Lula, 80, helped found the Workers’ Party under military rule and lost three presidential elections before winning in 2002. Jailed and barred from running in 2018, he returned to defeat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022 after his corruption convictions were annulled the previous year. He has now won an unprecedented fourth term.

Mr. Lula framed his candidacy as a way to defend democracy, protect Brazil’s sovereignty and prevent the Bolsonaro family’s return to power. Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, promised to restore his father’s conservative agenda while casting himself as a more moderate successor.

The result also halted a regional advance by the right. Although President Trump did not openly champion either candidate in Brazil, as he had in two other elections in Latin America, his administration tried in subtle ways to bolster Mr. Bolsonaro’s campaign.

Mr. Lula, who has repeatedly defied Mr. Trump, said the surge of rallies in the past week “was a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s backyard.” It was an apparent reference to the United States, which has been trying to exert new levels of control over Latin America through measures such as tariffs, sanctions and election intervention.

Mr. Lula’s margin of victory, 3.6 percentage points, was wider than it was four years ago. Few pollsters had predicted his comeback.

At a news conference, Mr. Bolsonaro refused to recognize the result and said he would seek to have the election annulled. He described the court’s decision to extend voting hours as a “dirty trick,” adding, “What happened today was not normal, and it was even unacceptable.”

Both candidates had requested the additional time. Mr. Bolsonaro said that flooding in a part of the country where he had strong support would unfairly hurt him, while Mr. Lula accused public officials of deliberately slowing public transportation in areas where he had won in the first round of voting.

A judge decided minutes before polls closed to extend hours at all polling stations. But by the time of the announcement, some polling centers had already closed and their voting machines had shut down, preventing them from reopening.

To seek to have the election annulled, Mr. Bolsonaro’s party will need to petition the authorities for a review of the results. Since Brazil’s return to democracy, no presidential election has been annulled.

In the 2014 election, the losing party requested an audit, but the review found no evidence of fraud and the results were upheld. In 2022, the Liberal Party similarly challenged Jair Bolsonaro’s election loss but failed to provide evidence to support its accusations and was fined by a court.

Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party has two possible paths to challenge the result, said Raquel Machado, a professor at the Federal University of Ceará. It could seek a technical audit to determine whether unequal voting conditions affected the outcome, potentially leading to an annulment of the election. Or it could pursue an abuse-of-power case through the Superior Electoral Court’s inspector general, which could disqualify Mr. Lula and his running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, even after they take office.

But Professor Machado noted that many polling stations had closed by the time the Supreme Court’s order was made public and that there had been no significant influx of voters after 5 p.m. local time.

Mr. Lula’s Workers’ Party could bring its own challenge over restrictions on public bus services on Election Day.

item.title: Chris Brown Gets Suspended Prison Sentence Over Nightclub Assault
item.description:
The pop star Chris Brown was given an eight-month suspended prison sentence on Monday over a 2023 episode in which he repeatedly hit a man in the head with a tequila bottle in a London nightclub.

The presiding judge, Tony Baumgartner, said in a hearing at Southwark Crown Court in London that the assault by Mr. Brown, 37, was “serious violence” that caused “obvious risk of more serious injury” to others in a crowded venue. The singer had to be pulled away to stop the attack, Judge Baumgartner added.

The judge said that Mr. Brown should not receive preferential treatment because of his fame but that there were mitigating factors, including the short duration of the assault and the singer’s low risk of reoffending.

As the sentence was announced, Mr. Brown looked relieved as he stood in a glass box at the back of the court with his hands clasped in front of him.

The sentencing came three months after Mr. Brown pleaded guilty to a charge of affray, or using or threatening unlawful violence. At a previous hearing, the singer had pleaded not guilty to a more serious charge of grievous bodily harm with intent.

In court on Monday, the prosecution played CCTV footage of the assault. It showed Mr. Brown and members of his entourage attacking Abraham Diaw, a music producer, in a busy club, and Mr. Brown swinging a bottle at Mr. Diaw, who was initially facing away from the singer.

One CCTV sequence showed Mr. Brown and his entourage following Mr. Diaw into a corridor and punching in his direction. The assault lasted about 20 seconds, the prosecution said.

In a news release after the sentencing, Christina Jessah of the Metropolitan Police in London described the assault as “an inexcusable attack that put a man in hospital.”

Under British sentencing guidelines for affray, the judge had discretion to impose a sentence ranging from a fine to three years’ imprisonment. The British government passed a law this year advising that shorter custodial sentences be suspended to reduce prison overcrowding.

Sallie Bennett-Jenkins, Mr. Brown’s lawyer, told the court before the sentencing that the singer had offered a “profound apology” for the “ugly and unattractive incident,” which she also described as a “very short-lived” event that did not cause any severe injuries.

Inside the court, about 20 fans of Mr. Brown watched the proceedings, some of whom said in interviews beforehand that they had traveled from northern England to see the sentencing. One fan outside the court held a homemade sign with a message to Mr. Brown saying, “We came from Italy.”

Shortly after the sentencing, Mr. Brown posted a video on Instagram in which he appeared to be in a car leaving court, and gave a thumbs up toward the camera.

The suspended sentence means that he can likely proceed with a 15-date stadium tour in the United States with the R&B star Usher that starts Nov. 5 in Atlanta.

The criminal sentence was not Mr. Brown’s first. In 2009, he pleaded guilty in a Los Angeles court to assaulting the singer Rihanna, his girlfriend at the time. In that case, the judge sentenced Mr. Brown to five years’ probation. He later served 108 days in jail for breaching his probation when he was thrown out of a rehabilitation center where he was being treated for anger management.

In 2014, at another court hearing, Mr. Brown pleaded guilty to punching a man in the face outside a hotel in downtown Washington and was sentenced to time served.

Ms. Bennett-Jenkins told the court on Monday that the judge should view those earlier convictions “through the prism of youth and immaturity.”

The latest altercation occurred at the Tape London nightclub on Feb. 19, 2023.

Mr. Brown’s vocal coach, Omololu Akinlolu, was also involved in the assault, punching Mr. Diaw in the head and kicking him when he was on the ground. Mr. Akinlolu also pleaded guilty to affray at a previous hearing, and on Monday the judge gave him a four-month suspended prison sentence.

item.title: Jordan Arrests 3 in Connection With Church Attack, State Media Reports
item.description:
Jordanian security forces arrested three men early Monday accused of carrying out an attack last week during a funeral at a church in southern Jordan that killed nine people, according to state media.

Security and commando forces captured the three suspects during a predawn raid on their hide-out in an abandoned house in Karak, the same southern province where the attack on a Greek Orthodox Church took place, according to Petra, the Jordanian state media service.

It said the suspects refused orders to surrender and opened fire, so the security forces responded in kind — wounding and disarming the three men before taking them into custody.

No security personnel were injured in the raid, Petra reported, adding that guns and ammunition were found inside the hide-out.

The suspects were not identified, and the authorities have not released details about what charges they will face.

The shooting in the village of Hamoud in southern Jordan was one of the deadliest attacks in the country in years.

Officials have not said exactly what motivated the deadly assault, which they called a terrorist attack. Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said at a news conference on Friday that it was “the result of terrorist takfiri ideology,” an Arabic term commonly used to describe Islamist extremists who declare other Muslims heretics.

“We have apprehended the killers, we are examining every factor that leads youth toward extremism, and we will hold accountable anyone proven to have been involved,” Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya wrote on social media on Monday.

The attack on Friday, which also injured nearly three dozen people, was met with widespread condemnation across Jordan. Officials vowed it would not divide Jordanians or threaten national stability.

King Abdullah II, who has ruled the kingdom through more than a quarter-century of regional upheaval, said on Friday that the attackers would be met with “the harshest retaliation.”

While Christians make up only about 2 percent of Jordan’s population, the country is home to some of the most important biblical and Christian pilgrimage sites, including what is said to be the location where Jesus was baptized. Christian Jordanians are guaranteed seats in Parliament and have long served as cabinet ministers and ambassadors.

The Christian presence in Karak dates back more than 1,500 years, to a time when the Eastern Roman Empire ruled that part of the Middle East.

Jordan, a close U.S. ally, has largely avoided the violence that has destabilized many of its neighbors, though it has faced sporadic militant attacks over the past decade. In 2016, Islamic State militants killed 10 people in a shooting rampage in and around the city of Karak before taking shelter in a medieval castle there.

item.title: María Corina Machado, Venezuela’s Leading Opposition Figure, Returns Home
item.description:
Venezuela’s most popular opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has returned to her country after nearly a year in exile, according to a spokesman.

The spokesman, David Smolansky, in a statement, called the return “a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future.”

Ms. Machado’s efforts to return to Venezuela have been fraught with political tension in recent months. The former member of Venezuela’s Legislature has led the opposition for the past three years, spending much of that time living in hiding inside her country, trying to avoid arrest.

She fled last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Then, after the United States captured Venezuela’s autocrat, Nicolás Maduro, in January in a raid on Caracas, the Trump administration chose to elevate another member of his repressive government, Delcy Rodríguez, to the presidency.

Tensions between the Trump administration and Ms. Machado have been high since.

Ms. Machado has repeatedly promised to return to her country and push for elections, telling The New York Times in a recent interview that her homecoming would arrive “sooner than you would expect.”

In a message on X at 11:31 a.m. Venezuela time, Ms. Machado wrote: “I am here. With you all.”

Her party also shared images of her in a church in Lara State, in the western part of the country, indicating that the photographs confirmed her arrival in Venezuela.

On Sunday after her announcement, President Trump told reporters in Washington: “She’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe, she’s a very nice woman. But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”

Mr. Smolansky, the aide to Ms. Machado, wrote in his statement: “We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the U.S. Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support.”

“Ms. Machado returns to stand with Venezuelans in their pursuit of freedom, democracy, and justice,” he added, “and to help advance a peaceful, inclusive, and sustainable transition leading to free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections, with guarantees for all.”

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Norway Pushes Back After Trump Disparages It Over Nobel Prize Decision
item.description:
President Trump was courteous toward Norway during his first term, describing it as a country the United States should accept more immigrants from. But on Sunday, two weeks after the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded its 2026 Peace Prize, he disparaged the country using a vulgar term for an outhouse.

“Frankly, Norway sucks,” Mr. Trump said at a campaign rally in Port Huron, Mich., on Sunday. “Norway has become a shithouse country, actually.”

He suggested that the United States should accept fewer Norwegian immigrants, saying, “I didn’t get the Nobel Prize.”

“So I don’t want anybody from Norway,” the president continued. “I don’t want anything to do with Norway.”

The Nobel Peace Prize — which the president has openly campaigned for — was awarded in Oslo to Navi Pillay, a South African human rights lawyer.

Mr. Trump’s remarks were met with bewilderment and exasperation in Norway, where top government officials have repeatedly said that they do not have influence over who is awarded the Peace Prize.

“He knows very well that the Nobel committee is independent,” Espen Barth Eide, the Norwegian foreign minister, told the country’s public broadcaster NRK on Monday. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering, and that is still the case.”

Norwegians on social media expressed their dismay at Mr. Trump’s remarks, although few seemed surprised. Some pointed out that Mr. Trump had described Norway in 2018 in glowing terms that were racially tinged when he contrasted the country with Haiti.

Norwegians generally view Mr. Trump’s public comments with some skepticism, said Eirik Lokke, an analyst at Civita, a centrist think tank in Oslo.

“We have simply grown accustomed to his erratic behavior and tend not to take every outburst too seriously,” he said.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement on Monday that it was “entirely independent of the Norwegian government.”

Norway’s Parliament appoints the committee’s five members for six-year terms. To protect the organization’s independence, members of the government have been barred from sitting on the committee since 1936 and incumbent lawmakers since 1977.

Mr. Trump has openly jockeyed for the Peace Prize for about a decade, mentioning it in dozens of interviews and speeches and also complaining about it privately. He described the committee’s decision this month to award Ms. Pillay the 2026 prize as “an indelible stain on Norway.”

In its announcement on Oct. 9, the Nobel committee said it was honoring Ms. Pillay, 85, for her efforts to promote international law. Over the years, she served as a top U.N. official and a judge on the International Criminal Court. Last year, she led a U.N. commission on Israel that said it was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a finding that Israel rejected.

At the rally on Sunday in Michigan, where the Trump ally Mike Rogers is locked in a close Senate contest with the Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the president returned again to the subject of the Nobel Prize, indicating that he had expected to be awarded it while also suggesting he had been too busy to give the issue much attention.

He repeated his claim that he had settled eight wars, which he has previously suggested should be rewarded with eight Nobel Peace Prizes. Several of the wars he has previously cited, including those between Israel and Hamas and between Israel and Iran, remain unresolved.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

item.title: Lula Wins Brazil’s Presidency, in Stunning Blow to Latin America’s Right
item.description:
Brazilian voters on Sunday handed the leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a fourth term in office and a surprise victory over Flávio Bolsonaro, his right-wing challenger, in a striking rebuke to a conservative surge sweeping Latin America.

Mr. Bolsonaro refused to accept the outcome and said it was the result of foul play, increasing the risk of unrest over the election result.

The rejection by voters of Mr. Bolsonaro, the son of a former president jailed for attempting a coup four years ago, is also a loss for President Trump, who had embraced the Bolsonaro family and the region’s rising right.

Mr. Lula, in contrast to many world leaders, has often and defiantly clashed with Mr. Trump, and his victory suggests that Latin America’s left-wing forces still wield influence despite a string of losses across the hemisphere. This is the first leftist victory following seven straight wins by right-wing leaders in the region over the last 18 months.

“I would like to thank the Brazilian people for the generosity they have shown me for a long time,” Mr. Lula said, during a victory speech in São Paulo, flanked by his wife, running mate and allies.

The result capped a chaotic final stretch of the race, as polling places were ordered to remain open after public transportation delays and torrential rains disrupted voting. The extended polling hours, which both candidates asked for but came right as voting was set to conclude, opened up the possibility that the results would be disputed.

Mr. Bolsonaro called an order by Brazil’s judiciary to extend voting a “dirty trick” and demanded the election be annulled.

“There’s a lot that needs to be cleared up before Brazil simply accepts this foul play that took place in these elections,” he said during a news conference in Brasília, the capital.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s party will now likely petition electoral authorities for a review of the result.

Since Brazil’s return to democracy, no presidential election has ever been annulled. In 2014, the losing party requested an audit, but that review found no evidence of fraud and the results were upheld.

In 2022, Mr. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party similarly challenged his father’s loss in the election, but the court ultimately fined the party more than $4 million for failing to provide evidence to support its allegations.

Among Mr. Bolsonaro’s supporters on Sunday, the sentiment was one of sadness and indignation. “We know we’ve been robbed again,” said Valéria Maria de Melo, a 49-year-old housewife, bursting into tears.

Mr. Lula headed into Sunday’s vote as the underdog after finishing 2 percentage points behind his opponent in the first round of voting earlier this month.

But on Sunday, Mr. Lula achieved a stunning comeback, winning 51.8 percent of the vote versus 48.2 percent for Flávio Bolsonaro, with nearly all the ballots counted.

Mr. Lula’s margin of victory on Sunday was roughly double the margin four years ago when he narrowly defeated Mr. Bolsonaro’s father. It was the first time in Brazil’s history that a candidate who lost the first round of voting came back to win the second.

Mr. Lula’s victory was even more surprising given that several of the candidates who failed to make it out of the first round were conservatives whose votes were expected to broadly shift to Mr. Bolsonaro.

Mr. Lula, speaking at a hotel surrounded by cheering allies and supporters, thanked those who had voted for him. In an indirect swipe at Mr. Trump, he said the mass rallies in Brazilian cities in the days leading up to the vote were “a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s backyard.”

“I want to thank the generosity of the Brazilian youth, who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he added.

The results suggested that far more voters had turned up to cast a ballot on Sunday than in the earlier round, a highly unusual shift. Typically, the number of voters drops from the first round to the second. In total, more than 128 million Brazilians voted on Sunday, compared to 125 million in the first round.

An intense social media campaign that included a wildly popular channel on WhatsApp, a platform long dominated by Mr. Bolsonaro’s right-wing movement, played a major role in mobilizing Mr. Lula’s supporters in the final stretch of the race.

As he celebrated in Rio de Janeiro, Fernando Porto said he and his friends never gave up hope as they took to social media and to the streets to rally support for Mr. Lula over the last three weeks. “This comeback was truly incredible,” said Mr. Porto, 24, a psychology student.

In São Paulo, a massive celebration that had already erupted long before the results came grew quickly with news of Mr. Lula’s victory. Supporters of the president broke down in tears of disbelief and set off fireworks, while cars honked in a deafening chorus of horns.

Mr. Lula’s comeback win capped a roller-coaster career for the president that has traversed soaring popularity, scandal and prison, and now an election that deeply divided Brazil, forcing voters to choose between two starkly different visions for the future of Latin America’s largest nation.

A stalwart of Brazilian politics, Mr. Lula lifted millions out of poverty through social programs in earlier years as president, though his popularity waned in his third term as he failed to address anxieties over crime and the economy.

His political legacy has also been tarnished by links to corruption scandals, including a new one unfolding on his watch that has implicated much of Brazil’s political and judicial elite, including Mr. Bolsonaro himself.

Yet Sunday’s narrow tally makes clear that Mr. Lula, 80, faces a daunting task: leading a polarized nation plagued by a spiraling debt crisis, high grocery prices and growing fears about organized crime. And Mr. Lula is bound to face resistance at every turn, after voters elected an overwhelming number of Mr. Bolsonaro’s political allies to the Legislature.

And the strong showing of Mr. Bolsonaro, 45, highlights that the right-wing leader’s ideas resonate with millions of working-class Brazilians who may have supported Mr. Lula in the past, but have become disillusioned with him.

Ultimately, though, a majority of voters appears to have heeded Mr. Lula’s warnings about handing power to another Bolsonaro, just four years after former President Jair Bolsonaro orchestrated a plan to hold onto the presidency and inspired supporters to storm Brazil’s halls of power.

Last year, the elder Mr. Bolsonaro was sentenced to 27 years in prison for trying to stage a coup after the 2022 election, in a plot that included plans to assassinate Mr. Lula, Mr. Lula’s running mate and a Supreme Court justice.

The younger Mr. Bolsonaro had said he planned to seek amnesty for his father and the rioters, impeach the Supreme Court justice who oversaw their jailing, and change the nation’s constitution.

Mr. Lula’s resounding win on Sunday signals that the majority of Brazilians want to protect their democracy, said Christian Lynch, a political scientist at the State University of Rio de Janeiro.

“People here realized they don’t want to surrender democracy,” he said. “It was a big surprise.”

Mr. Lula’s win will most likely complicate Mr. Trump’s plans for dominance in the region: The Brazilian leader has repeatedly defied Mr. Trump over issues like trade, social media and the treatment of the Bolsonaros.

Mr. Trump remained silent about Mr. Lula’s win on Sunday. While he had not formally endorsed Mr. Bolsonaro, his administration had appeared willing to help him in other ways, such as by labeling Brazil’s largest drug gangs as terror groups. Last year, the American president also tried, and failed, to help Mr. Bolsonaro’s father avoid jail by hitting Brazil with tariffs and sanctions.

Turning Brazilian sovereignty into a rallying cry, Mr. Lula repeatedly urged voters to reject the younger Mr. Bolsonaro, painting him as a puppet of the United States.

Sunday’s result signaled that many Brazilians had rejected Mr. Bolsonaro’s cozy ties with the United States.

Despite Mr. Lula’s disagreements with Mr. Trump, Brazil’s economy was largely unscathed by American tariffs during his third term, and unemployment dropped to record-low rates. But rising food prices and mounting household debt have weighed heavily on Mr. Lula’s approval ratings.

Many Brazilians are also eager to see if Mr. Lula makes good on his promises for a judicial overhaul amid a crisis of confidence in Brazil’s top court. The next president will have unusually broad power to shape the court, which has 11 members, by filling up to four seats freed by justices reaching the mandatory retirement age.

“Most people want change,” said Thomas Traumann, a political analyst and press secretary for a former leftist Brazilian president, “but not the Bolsonaro change.”

Reporting was contributed by Giovana Sanchez in São Paulo; Thayz Guimarães in Brasília; Silvia Ribeiro, Leonardo Coelho, Isabela Cruz and Lis Moriconi in Rio de Janeiro; Naira Hofmeister in Pôrto Alegre.

item.title: Egypt Approves Sending Military Support to Defend Saudi Arabia From Houthis
item.description:
Egypt’s Parliament authorized the country’s military on Monday to provide support to Saudi Arabia in its escalating war against the Iranian-backed Houthi militia, Egyptian state media said.

The move, requested by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi last week, risks drawing the Arab world’s most populous nation deeper into regional turmoil at a time when U.S. and Israeli officials are said to be drawing up plans for renewed attacks on Iran.

Egyptian officials have stressed that the military support will be purely defensive. Mr. el-Sisi said last week that Egyptian forces would operate only inside Saudi borders, and would not be involved in direct attacks on Houthi targets in Yemen, according to state news media.

In a statement, the Parliament said that the military support was aimed at “defending the kingdom’s territory, sovereignty and holy sites against any external aggression.”

Saudi Arabia has not commented on the Egyptian Parliament’s decision, and neither country has publicly confirmed a Saudi request for Egyptian military assistance. The kingdom has in recent weeks exchanged increasingly deadly strikes with the Houthis, who have hit Saudi airports and oil sites.

As the conflict escalated, President Trump rebuffed Saudi appeals last month to launch U.S. strikes against the Houthis. But the United States is providing significant military support, including intelligence in support of the kingdom’s Yemeni allies and refueling for Saudi warplanes conducting defensive air patrols, according to one current and one former U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters. And last week, the British government said it would send fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia’s cities and critical infrastructure.

Egypt had long sought to stay out of rising regional tensions, and to instead support diplomatic initiatives to end the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. That position may have become less tenable as the Saudi-Houthi conflict began threatening shipping through the Red Sea, a vital waterway for global trade that feeds into Egypt’s Suez Canal.

Saudi Arabia is also an important regional ally for Egypt and an important economic backer. Hundreds of thousands of Egyptians work in the kingdom and send remittances back home.

“Egypt can’t afford to let Saudi descend into deeper instability,” said H.A. Hellyer, a senior associate fellow focused on Middle East security at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based research center. “From Egypt’s point of view, it is reliant on Saudi Arabia being a strong linchpin of the regional security order.”

The decision to send forces to Saudi Arabia is nonetheless fraught for Egyptians, who have not forgotten Egypt’s long and costly involvement in Yemen’s civil war of the 1960s, when tens of thousands of troops were deployed in the country.

Critics have since argued that it severely drained Egypt’s finances and military preparedness for its 1967 war with Israel, when Israel seized the Sinai Peninsula and occupied it for over a decade.

On Monday, with the Parliament expected to make a decision on whether to commit military support, Egypt’s pound hit record lows against the dollar.

Though it remains unclear how many troops Egypt will send to Saudi Arabia, the decision is nonetheless a symbolic boost for the kingdom as it seeks to garner regional and international support.

Egypt’s Parliament began debating the authorization in two closed-door sessions last week at Mr. el-Sisi’s request. The final vote on Monday required at least two-thirds of lawmakers to endorse the decision.

Earlier this month, Egypt’s National Defense Council, whose chairman is Mr. el-Sisi, said that Egypt would provide “all necessary and possible forms of support” to defend the kingdom but did not specify what that would entail.

When Saudi Arabia led a yearslong military intervention against the Houthis in 2015, after the militia seized control of the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, Egypt contributed air and naval support. Egyptian warships also helped protect shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

In recent months, that strait has again become a point of contention.

In July, the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, firing on passing tankers. Then last month, they staged a lightning advance along Yemen’s coast, seizing territory adjacent to the Bab al-Mandab from the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

The threat to Red Sea shipping is of critical concern to Egypt. The Suez Canal is a major source of foreign currency. Yet some Egyptians remain wary of the decision to send forces to fight another Arab force, particularly as it risks embroiling their country in the broader regional conflict.

One lawmaker, Abdel-Alim Dawood, told an Egyptian newspaper, Al-Masry Al-Youm, that he declined to vote, fearing “an explosion in the region that would serve Israel’s interests.”

]]>
